# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is a catalogue of the visual forms the sciences use to organise what
they know — roughly a hundred of them, from Playfair's bars to the Higgs bump.
Each form is reproduced from data and code, not reprinted; each carries a
citable account of where it came from; and the whole set is arranged in a
single teaching order that runs from the raw perceptual channels a mark can
exploit, through the Gestalt principles that let marks group into structure,
to the dynamic and uncertain territory beyond the static frame.

Two disciplines govern every entry. The figure is **reproduced, never
reprinted** — the historical originals are frequently under copyright, so each
is redrawn from data or a faithful model instance, with the original described
in prose and cited. And the provenance is **citable, never asserted** — an
entry is not finished until its canonical-introduction citation resolves in
the bibliography. Where the first appearance and the canonical reference are
different documents (they often are), both are given and kept distinct.

The book renders from one set of sources to two targets: the online edition
you may be reading now, and a print edition built with LuaLaTeX. Every figure
is generated by the executable code shown with it.

## How to read the Atlas

Each entry follows one fixed template — provenance class, canonical
introduction, domain, a gloss of one or two sentences, then the reproduction —
so the set reads as a catalogue, not an anthology. The provenance classes are
defined at the head of the Atlas. Entries are numbered 1–103 and sit under
unit headings that carry the perceptual argument; the AIATSIS map of
Indigenous Australia stands before them all as an acknowledgement of the
country on which this book was written.
